title: Political ‘flag’ football, Cap’n Bobby claims credit and Ellis can be quiet, in political notes
summary: Sen. J.B. Jennings wants the Maryland flag written into the Maryland Constitution, Bobby LaPin claims credit where critics say it's not due, and Sen. Arthur Ellis' protest over redistricting ends quietly in the Maryland Senate, in political notes.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters March 10, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters March 10, 2026

The Maryland flag needs protecting.

So says Sen. J.B. Jennings (R-Baltimore and Harford), who introduced a bill Monday that would enshrine the flag – already a state symbol — into the Maryland Constitution.

“We’ve enshrined a lot of things in our constitution — recently, abortion, marijuana and gambling,” Jennings said. “All this does is, basically it enshrines the flag that we know and love.”

Jennings said he was moved to introduce the bill after comments made by Gov. Wes Moore (D). “Ideas start with a spark,” Jennings said.

Moore, appearing on a podcast last month, mentioned the flag and its “complicated history” while answering a question about whether the country would accept another Black president. From that, some inferred that Moore was at best calling the flag a vestige of the Confederacy and at worst, racist.

“Sometimes change is good, sometimes change is bad,” Jennings said. “On this one, I think that one change would be bad, and that would be our state flag. Earlier this year, there were thoughts about possibly changing the state flag, or thoughts about it in speculation.

“What this would do is protect it, the flag we love so much,” said Jennings, who sported a Maryland flag tie Monday for the occasion.

For the record, Moore did not call for changing the flag.

Soon after the comments were reported, Moore told reporters he loved the flag. A spokesperson dismissed criticisms as unfounded and the continued conversation about the flag as “silly.”

Moore even mentioned the flag both in a CBS town hall and in his State of the State address: “I love our flag. And to be clear, it ain’t changing.”

The timing of Jennings’ introduction of the bill was important for two reasons.

First, it was the 122nd anniversary of the Maryland General Assembly’s adoption of the current flag as a state symbol on March 9, 1904.

Second, the deadline for introducing bills passed at 4 p.m. Monday. Jenning’s late introduction — there are just five weeks left in the 2026 session — meant that Jennings had to stand and explain his bill and ask for a suspension of the chamber rules Monday. It also means the bill will be assigned to the Senate Rules Committee, where its future is anything but assured.

When Baltimore Gas & Electric announced last week that it was “temporarily pausing” a controversial underground power line project in South Baltimore, it came just days after Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) took a stand against the project.

But Ferguson’s challenger, social media personality and charter boat captain Bobby LaPin, claimed credit for the pause, too.

“With one social media post that received hundreds of thousands of views, Bobby LaPin’s grassroots movement to pause BGE’s unnecessary half-billion dollar Baltimore Peninsula project forced Bill Ferguson to take a stand against utility monopoly,” read a campaign message sent to LaPin’s supporters.

Not so fast, say neighborhood leaders in South Baltimore, several of whom appeared alongside Ferguson at a news conference in the neighborhood opposing the construction.

“Unlike Senator Ferguson, Mr. LaPin did not engage with our local community associations who have been doing the real work on this issue. Social media posts are not the same as real grassroots efforts by your friends and neighbors,” read a letter from the neighborhood associations in Otterbein, Ridgely’s Delight and other neighborhoods affected by the proposed project.

LaPin argues that even though Ferguson worked with the community associations, it was his advocacy on social media, paired with his election year challenge to the Senate president, that spurred Ferguson to take action. Across platforms including Instagram, Reddit and Facebook, LaPin said his video about the project was viewed by several hundred thousand people.

“At the end of the day, I just believe it was an all-encompassing community effort,” LaPin said.

The one-man protest over midcycle redistricting started last month by Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles) is over. It took two days to notice.

Reporters on the Senate floor Monday night noticed the green light next to Ellis’ name during three quorum calls. It’s a light that had not been lit since Ellis demanded a month ago that the full Senate be allowed to vote on a congressional redistricting bill passed by the House. He punctuated the demand by walking off the floor.

After, he said he would protest until the bill was out of the Senate Rules Committee — a sort of legislative Elba Island for late filed or unwanted bills.

The protest was always mostly symbolic.

And as the days ticked by, and the redistricting bill remained in committee, Ellis softened his approach. At one point he asked to have his presence recorded even though he was not signing in electronically.

Then, he just stopped.

Ellis, speaking Monday night, acknowledged the end to his protest. He pointed out that the official end came on Friday.

“Ellis can be quiet,” he said.

The bill remains in committee.

Ellis compared the end of his protest to a scene in the movie “Forrest Gump.”

“Remember that scene where he just ran and ran, ran, and then he just stopped, just stopped, turns around and he said, I’m going to go home now?” Ellis said.

“I ran until I stopped,” he said.
